title: OpenTLP device entry
description:
The front matter of one device page. Modelled on OpenWrt's Table of Hardware dataentry, which likewise sits inside an ordinary wiki page: the structured fields here feed the table and the JSON export, while the Markdown body below them carries the prose a field cannot hold.

The governing rule is that every field is a CHECKABLE CLAIM. If nobody has verified it, leave it out — an absent field reads as 'unknown', which is honest, while a guessed one reads as fact and is not. `sources` exists so a reader can audit any row back to where it came from.

id.description: Stable slug, conventionally <brand>_<model>. Never reused or renumbered: external projects key off it.

brand.description: The name on the box. This is often NOT the manufacturer — see `rebadge_of`.

model.description: Model as printed on the device or its packaging.

aliases.description: Other names the same hardware is sold under. Distinct from `rebadge_of`, which points at the entry this one is a copy of.

rebadge_of.description:
The `id` of the device this is a rebadge of.

Rebadging is rampant in this market: one ODM's hardware is sold under dozens of brands, and a single brand may span several unrelated protocols. Recording it is the difference between a catalogue of 150 printers and a catalogue of 9 printers with 150 stickers.

manufacturer.description:
Who actually makes it, where known and different from `brand`.

A high bar. A certification filing names whoever placed the device on that market, which is often an importer; a vendor app's publisher is a software company that may or may not be the factory. Record this only where a source says so directly, and leave it out otherwise — an unattributed device is a normal state in this market.

summary.description: One line for the table and the top of the page. Anything longer belongs in the page body, which is what the prose is for.

artwork.description:
An illustration of the printer.

A line drawing that shows the shape of the machine, its paper path and its controls does more to confirm 'yes, that is the one on my desk' than any specification row. SVG rather than a photograph because it scales, stays legible in dark mode, weighs almost nothing, and can be recoloured by whatever consumes it.

Unlike everything else in this database, artwork is a creative work and IS copyrightable — hence `licence` is required, and hence contributed artwork must be original or already free. A photograph lifted from a shop listing is not.

file.description: Filename beside this page, e.g. 'marklife_p12.svg'. Sanitised at build time: scripts, event handlers, external references and animation are stripped, so submit inert artwork and expect anything clever to be removed.

licence.description: SPDX id. 'CC0-1.0' for work contributed here under the project's default terms.

credit.description: Who drew it, where attribution is required or simply deserved.

source.description: Where it came from, if not drawn for this database.

variants.description:
Colourways the model is actually sold in.

Listed as whole pairings rather than as independent colour choices, because a shell and a cutter moulded in different colours do not mix freely — a reader must not be shown a product that does not exist.

Each variant sets CSS custom properties on the drawing, which is why the artwork is inlined rather than linked: one file renders every variation.

properties.description: CSS custom properties the drawing reads, e.g. '--printer-body'. Published rather than assumed, so a consumer binds to a name the artwork guarantees.

hooks.description:
How the drawing exposes its moving and recolourable parts, keyed by part name.

Published rather than assumed, so a consumer binds to a name the artwork guarantees instead of one it hopes for — and so a newly added printer works in an interface that already knows how to drive a cutter.

animations.description:
Movements the drawing can depict.

Here rather than in `mechanism` because nobody reads a spec table to learn how far a lever travels — the numbers exist so a picture can move correctly, and they are useless without the artwork they drive.

Still described as part positions and real durations rather than as CSS. Whether to play a movement at all, how fast, and what to do under a reduced-motion preference is left to whatever renders it.

lamps.description:
Lit states the drawing can depict, keyed to the hook that colours them.

The split from `indicators` is deliberate and worth keeping. `indicators` records what each colour *means* on this machine — documentation, and the thing a reader searches for. This records what the *drawing* has to be told to show one, which is a property of the artwork and changes when the artwork is redrawn.

A consumer that wants to depict a live printer joins the two on `state`.

protocol.description: How to talk to it. The single most valuable thing in this database, and the hardest to obtain.

family.description: Protocol family slug, e.g. 'tiny', 'niimbot', 'esc-pos', 'tspl', 'zpl', 'brother-raster', 'marklife-1f'. Devices sharing a family are driven by the same code.

variant.description: Sub-variant within the family, where one exists.

packet_prefix.description: Leading bytes of every command packet, lowercase hex, space separated. e.g. '51 78'.

vendor_app.description:
Android package of the manufacturer's own app, e.g. 'com.frogtosea.tinyPrint'.

Empirically the best single predictor of which protocol a device speaks — better than the brand on the case, because the app ships the firmware's own driver.

width_dots.description: Printable width in dots. 384 is the 58 mm norm.

media_width_mm.description: Widest media the mechanism accepts, which is usually wider than the printable area.

media.description:
Media types the firmware can detect and index.

Beyond the usual paper: 'heat-shrink' and 'pvc-tag' are stock a label printer is not obviously expected to take, and knowing a machine handles them is often the reason somebody chooses it. 'black-mark-gap' is a distinct sensing mode, not a shorthand for supporting both.

colour.description: Two-colour stock develops a second colour at a different temperature; it is not a second ink.

colour_planes.description:
How many separable colours the mechanism can develop in one pass.

One for ordinary thermal stock. Two for two-colour paper, where a second colour appears at a different temperature — which is a property of the paper and the head's ability to reach that temperature, not a second ink. Recorded separately from `colour` because software needs the count to decide how many planes to render, and the word 'two-colour' does not give it a number.

max_density.description:
Highest density value the protocol accepts.

A fact about the command set, not a preference: sending a higher value is out of range. The default a piece of software chooses within that range is its own business and does not belong here.

speed_mode.description:
Whether the device accepts a print-speed command.

Separate from `mechanism.print_speed_mm_s`, which is how fast it runs. This says only whether the speed is settable at all — the difference between a driver that can offer the choice and one that must not.

mechanism.description: How the paper path behaves. These are the facts that decide whether a label comes out usable, and almost none of them can be inferred from the protocol — they have to be observed on the machine.

cutter.description:
Whether the printer has a cutter at all.

Deliberately a yes/no. Whether the operator works a lever or the firmware drives it barely matters to anyone choosing or driving the machine; whether there is one at all decides how every label comes off the roll.

Worth stating even when the answer is no, because product photography routinely shows a cutter the shipped hardware does not have.

head_to_cutter_dots.description:
Distance from the print head to wherever the label is separated, in dots.

The most consequential number in this section: feed less than this and the finished label is still inside the machine. It also sets how much blank stock every job wastes. Recorded in dots because that is what a driver feeds; the millimetre equivalent follows from the resolution.

backfeed.description:
Whether the printer retracts media back under the head before printing. Also called pullback.

A printer that feeds out for tearing and then backfeeds starts the next label at the head and wastes nothing. One that does not leaves a fixed gap at the top of every label, and software has to allow for it — which is why this is a yes/no worth stating rather than leaving to be discovered.

paper_drm.description:
Whether the printer checks its consumables and refuses unknown stock — paper DRM.

'circumventable' means a check exists but third-party stock works anyway; 'strict' means it does not. Frequently the field that decides whether the printer is worth buying, and the one manufacturers are least forthcoming about, so it is worth stating even when the answer is 'none'.

print_speed_mm_s.description: Nominal speed at default density, in millimetres per second.

media_widths_mm.description: Stock the mechanism accepts: one fixed width, or a range for printers with adjustable guides.

connectivity.description: At least one way in, or the entry cannot help anybody.

name_pattern.description:
Regular expression matched against the advertised BLE name.

A regex rather than a prefix list because prefixes are not the real rule: `P12` and `P12_` differ by firmware, `LY01`-`LY05` and `LY10`-`LY11` speak different dialects despite the shared stem, and matching `D11` loosely also catches `D110`.

**Leave it unanchored unless you have seen the name.** These printers routinely advertise a model string with a serial or MAC fragment appended, so an anchored `^GB01$` fails on a real `GB01-4F2A`, and even `^GB01` assumes the model comes first. An unanchored pattern says only 'the name contains this', which is usually all anyone actually knows. Anchoring is a claim about the exact form, and needs an observed example behind it.

Keep it portable — JavaScript, Python and Dart all consume this — so no lookbehind and no named groups.

name_examples.description:
Names actually observed in a scan.

Their absence is meaningful: a pattern with no examples has been inferred from a model number rather than seen, and both the validator and the rendered page say so. They also make the table searchable, since nobody types a regex into a search box.

battery_cell.description: Cell type or format, e.g. '18650', 'Li-Po pouch'. Relevant because a replaceable cell decides whether the printer outlives its battery.

mains_only.description: True for desktop units with no battery at all.

hardware.description: Physical and internal facts, generally established by opening the case or reading a certification filing.

mcu.description: Microcontroller, as marked on the die or the silkscreen.

certification.description: Regulatory filings. Far more useful than they sound: an FCC id opens a public record of internal photographs, block diagrams and the manual, which is often the only primary documentation a cheap printer has.

indicators.description:
Lights and displays, and what they mean.

One of the most searched-for facts about any cheap printer and one of the least documented: the manual is a folded sheet, and 'what does the flashing red light mean' is where most owners start. Recording it costs a line and answers the question permanently.

Distinct from `reports`, which is what the printer says over the wire. An indicator is what it says to the room.

reports.description:
What the printer volunteers about itself.

This is the difference between a machine you can build a decent interface for and one you can only write to and hope. List only what has actually been seen coming back — an empty or absent list means nobody has checked, not that the printer is silent.

support.description:
Cross-project support matrix, keyed by project slug (e.g. 'blewebler2', 'cat-printer', 'timini-print', 'niimblue', 'phomemo-tools').

This is the part no single project can maintain about itself honestly, and the main reason this database is worth keeping separate from any one of them.

status.description:
How much to trust this entry as a whole.

'verified' means somebody printed from it and said so. 'reported' means a credible second-hand account. 'unverified' means transcribed from a catalogue or inferred. Most entries start unverified and that is fine — pretending otherwise is not.

sources.description: Where the claims above came from. Required, because an unsourced hardware database is a rumour with a table around it.

documentation.description:
External documentation that goes deeper than this entry ever should.

Some communities maintain excellent per-brand wikis — teardowns, PCB shots, firmware notes. Duplicating them here would be worse than useless: it would go stale while looking authoritative. Link out instead, and keep this database to the structured fields that a table and an importer can actually use.

level.description: 'listed' means the project names the model but successful output has not been evidenced here. 'works' requires someone to have printed successfully. 'partial' means it prints but something is wrong or missing.

driver.description: Driver or module name inside that project.

id.description: Stable name for this source within the entry. Useful when prose or review discussion needs to identify which evidence supports a claim.

kind.description: What sort of evidence this is. A protocol capture and a shop listing are not the same weight of claim, and the table should not pretend they are.

licence.description: SPDX id where the source is a project. Recorded so a reader can tell whether they may take code from it, not just facts.

covers.description: Dotted field paths this source supports, for example 'print.width_dots', 'mechanism.cutter', or 'support.niimblue'. A parent path such as 'print' covers its recorded children. Omit rather than guessing when the source's scope has not yet been audited.

licence.description: SPDX id. Recorded because a reader may want to reuse what they find there, and share-alike terms travel.

note.description: Why this link is here, when that is not obvious — for instance that it documents a near neighbour rather than this exact device.

holder.description:
The company named on the filing.

This is whoever took regulatory responsibility for placing the device on that market, which may be the manufacturer, the brand, or an importer or distributor — a European company on a filing for hardware built in Shenzhen is placing it on the market, not building it. Useful as a lead and as a way to link rebadges that share a filing; not evidence of who manufactures.

colours.description: Custom property name without the leading dashes, mapped to a colour. Sampled from the product, not invented — a UI green is not a pastel mint.

kind.description: 'smd-single-colour' is one emitter that lights one wavelength at a time. It matters: software must never blend two of its colours or show both at once, because that would depict a part the printer does not have.

unlit.description: How the part looks with no power, which is also the artwork's resting state.

colour.description: Colour name as a person would say it: red, green, blue, amber, white.

hex.description: What it actually emits, for artwork and for telling two greens apart.

pattern.description: Steady and flashing routinely mean different things on the same colour — on many of these printers red is 'charging' and flashing red is 'nearly flat'. Recording only the colour loses half the signal.

means.description: What the machine is telling you.

class.description: Class on the SVG group, so a consumer can target the part without knowing its shape.

property.description: CSS custom property that drives it.

units_per_mm.description: SVG user units per millimetre in this drawing, so millimetres from `mechanism` can be converted without knowing how the artwork was scaled.

label.description: What a control triggering it should say.

part.description: Which hook it drives, keyed into `artwork.hooks`.

travel_mm.description: Displacement from rest at the extreme of the movement. Positive is downward.

duration_ms.description: How long the real mechanism takes.

returns_to_rest.description: False leaves the part parked, which is a state change rather than a gesture.

hook.description: Key into `artwork.hooks` naming the part this colours.

unlit.description: The part with no power, which is the drawing's resting state.

states.description:
State name mapped to the colour the drawing should use for it. Names should match the `colour` values under `indicators`, so the two join.

On a single-colour emitter exactly one of these applies at a time: blending two, or showing both, depicts a part the printer does not have.
